_doc: Three registers for every skill. A standard code is an internal identifier and must never reach a child's eyes. `kid` is what an 8-11 year old sees; `teacher` is the professional label; `reteach` is what a teacher would actually DO about it in class, which is the only part of a diagnosis they can act on. Hand-authored for the fractions corridor; the rest of the 77-node cone still needs generating.

_registers.kid: Plain, concrete, no jargon. 'Bottom number', not 'denominator'.
_registers.teacher: Precise professional wording. Jargon is correct here.
_registers.reteach: A concrete classroom move, not a restatement of the standard.

5.NF.A.1.kid: Adding fractions with different bottom numbers
5.NF.A.1.teacher: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators
5.NF.A.1.reteach: Before any common-denominator procedure, check they can say WHY fourths and sixths cannot be counted together. Most who fail here can execute the algorithm but cannot explain it.

5.NF.A.2.kid: Fraction word problems with different bottom numbers
5.NF.A.2.teacher: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators
5.NF.A.2.reteach: Have them estimate first: is the answer more or less than one? Catches the add-the-denominators error instantly.

4.NF.B.3.d.kid: Fraction word problems where the bottoms match
4.NF.B.3.d.teacher: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators
4.NF.B.3.d.reteach: Keep the denominator fixed and vary the story. Isolates the language from the arithmetic.

4.NF.B.3.b.kid: Breaking a fraction into smaller pieces
4.NF.B.3.b.teacher: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator
4.NF.B.3.b.reteach: 3/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4, with a bar model beside it. Decomposition is what makes addition make sense later.

4.NF.B.3.a.teacher: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole
4.NF.B.3.a.reteach: Stress 'the same whole'. Half a small pizza and half a large one is where this breaks.

4.NF.A.1.kid: Why 1/2 and 2/4 are the same amount
4.NF.A.1.teacher: Explain why a/b is equivalent to (n x a)/(n x b) using visual fraction models
4.NF.A.1.reteach: Fold the same strip twice. The amount did not change, only the number of cuts. Students who 'know' equivalence often think the fraction got bigger.

4.NF.A.2.teacher: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators
4.NF.A.2.reteach: Benchmark against 1/2 before cross-multiplying. Procedure without benchmarks fails on 5/8 vs 4/7.

3.NF.A.3.kid: Fractions that look different but are worth the same
3.NF.A.3.teacher: Explain equivalence of fractions in special cases, and compare fractions by reasoning about their size
3.NF.A.3.reteach: Same-size wholes, different cuts, side by side. Comparison is meaningless if the wholes differ.

3.NF.A.2.kid: Finding fractions on a number line
3.NF.A.2.teacher: Understand a fraction as a number on the number line
3.NF.A.2.reteach: The jump from 'fraction as shaded pizza' to 'fraction as a number' is a real conceptual leap. Number lines are where fractions stop being pictures.

3.NF.A.1.kid: Cutting a whole into equal parts
3.NF.A.1.teacher: Understand a fraction 1/b as one part when a whole is partitioned into b EQUAL parts
3.NF.A.1.reteach: Show a shape cut into 4 unequal pieces and ask if the shaded one is a quarter. The word 'equal' is doing all the work in this standard and is the single most-skipped idea in elementary fractions.
3.NF.A.1.concrete: 1/4 means one of four SAME-SIZE parts

2.G.A.3.teacher: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares
2.G.A.3.reteach: Physical folding, not worksheets. This is where 'equal' first has to mean equal.

2.G.A.2.kid: Splitting a rectangle into equal squares
2.G.A.2.teacher: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count them
2.G.A.2.reteach: Links partitioning to area and later to multiplication.

2.MD.A.2.kid: Measuring the same thing with different rulers
2.MD.A.2.teacher: Measure the length of an object twice using different length units; describe how the measurements relate
2.MD.A.2.reteach: Bigger unit, smaller number. This inverse relationship IS the denominator idea, three years early, and almost nobody connects the two.

2.MD.A.1.teacher: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools
2.MD.A.1.reteach: Watch for starting at 1 instead of 0.

1.G.A.3.teacher: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares; describe using halves and fourths
1.G.A.3.reteach: Vocabulary plus fair-sharing language: 'would that be fair?' is the most reliable prompt at this age.

3.OA.A.1.teacher: Interpret products of whole numbers as equal groups
3.OA.A.1.reteach: 5 x 7 as five groups of seven. Equal groups is the same idea as equal parts, in a different costume.

3.MD.C.5.teacher: Recognize area as an attribute of plane figures and understand concepts of area measurement
3.MD.C.5.reteach: Tiling with no gaps or overlaps. Same 'equal units' principle again.
